content_metadata.description: Conference presentation on the adsorption of heavy metals from pharmaceutical wastewater using a silver-clay composite.

qAndA.answer: The plant species used was Parkia biglobosa, also known as the African locust bean tree. This information is visible in the 'Methodology' slide flowchart.
qAndA.question: What plant species was used to reduce silver ions into silver nanoparticles?

qAndA.answer: The average particle size is 42.90 nanometers. This is mentioned in the 'Results and Discussion' slide and visible in the text accompanying the SEM image.
qAndA.question: What is the average particle size of the silver nanoparticles loaded onto the clay?

qAndA.answer: Clay was chosen because nanoparticles tend to aggregate in solution, making separation difficult. Supporting them on clay prevents aggregation and aids in post-separation. This is explained in the 'Justification' slide.
qAndA.question: Why was clay chosen as a support for the silver nanoparticles?

qAndA.answer: The optimal adsorbent dosage was 0.4 grams. This is shown in the graph labeled 'Results of Adsorption Kinetics' in the 'Results and Discussion (Cont'd)' slide.
qAndA.question: What was the optimal adsorbent dosage identified in the study?

qAndA.answer: They used several characterization techniques, including X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). This information is presented in the 'Results and Discussion' slides.
qAndA.question: How did the researchers confirm the successful loading of silver nanoparticles onto the clay?

youtube_description: Clay supported silver nanoparticles were green synthesized using the aqueous leaf extract of Parkia biglobosa. The phytochemical analysis and FTIR results of the Parkia biglobosa showed that the leaf contains phenol, tanning, and flavonoids, which act as reducing, capping and stabilizing agents required for the synthesis of the silver nanoparticles. The prepared adsorbent has good morphology, is rich in silica, and contains functional groups suitable for heavy metal binding. The adsorptions of Zn, Cu, and Pb from pharmaceutical wastewater onto the silver-modified clay were studied as an adsorbent dosage and contact time. From the percentage removal results obtained, the adsorbent had up to 99.96%, 99.5%, and 99.44% removal efficiency for Zn, Pb, and Cu, respectively. The present work shows that the synthesized silver nanoparticles supported on local clay can be used as a potentially low-cost adsorbent to remove heavy metal ions from industrial wastewater.
